title: EF status, detail rows, and forms tools lack pagination — paginated contract is uneven
description: Round-1 P14-014 added limit/offset pagination to `lacerte_client_list` and `lacerte_table_read`. But the six per-row reads — `lacerte_ef_status`, `lacerte_detail_read`, `lacerte_forms_read`, `lacerte_subclient_read`, `lacerte_state_read`, `lacerte_state_subclient_read`, `lacerte_status_read` — were NOT updated and still return the entire result set with a `count` field but no `total`/`limit`/`offset`/`hasMore`/`nextOffset`. This is the response-shape inconsistency that DECISIONS.md "Pagination contract" landed in round 1, but the contract is half-applied. The model has to learn two paged response shapes for tools in the same family, and a partnership with 100 partners or a return with 2000 detail rows blows through the LLM's context window with no escape. The audit-findings P14-038 ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md update mentions the pagination shape but doesn't enforce it across all read tools.
recommendation: Apply the same `Pagination.Page<T>` wrapper to ALL six read tools above with the response shape `{rows, total, limit, offset, hasMore, nextOffset}` plus the legacy `count` for v0.1 backwards-compat. Update each tool's Description attribute to mention limit/offset. The cost is small (the pagination utility already exists; each tool is a 4-line change), and the contract becomes uniform — the model can paginate any read with one mental model. Add a paginated-contract assertion to ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md that every `lacerte_*_read` / `lacerte_*_list` tool returns the same six fields. Either expose a `Series`/`Code` filter (per finding 2) OR pagination — without either, `lacerte_detail_read` is unusable on real returns.
rationale: The pagination contract is a project-wide promise that's currently honored by 2/8 read tools. Inconsistency in tool surfaces makes the model fall back to overfetch on the un-paginated tools, which defeats the entire pagination story.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by direct file reads. The six tools — EFileTools.LacerteEfStatus (returns {count, efStatuses}), DetailsTools.LacerteDetailRead ({clientNumber, count, rows}), FormsTools.LacerteFormsRead ({clientNumber, count, forms}), SubclientsTools.LacerteSubclientRead ({clientNumber, count, subclients}), StatesTools.LacerteStateRead + LacerteStateSubclientRead ({..., count, states/stateSubclients}), and StatusTools.LacerteStatusRead ({clientNumber, count, statuses}) — all return unpaginated envelopes with only a `count` field. Pagination.Page<T> exists at src/LacertMCP.Server/Pagination/Pagination.cs and emits the canonical {Rows, Total, Limit, Offset, HasMore, NextOffset} shape. F13 (Todo.md line 170) explicitly states only `lacerte_client_list` + `lacerte_table_read` were retrofitted and notes "Existing tools NOT yet retrofitted." Phase-14 P14-014 was scoped to lacerte_client_list only. P14-036 acknowledged the post-pagination shape but only updated ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA for #42 and #43 — the per-client read sections (#44-47, #49) still document the legacy `{count, ...}` shape (verified at ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md lines 62, 67-68, 73, 79, 85). No Phase-14 task or F-followup item covers these six. The finding is genuinely new, not a duplicate. Fully sim-actionable: the pagination utility exists, each tool is a ~4-line change, and the tests are off-Windows. One nuance worth noting in the refinement: lacerte_ef_status reads ALL eFilings in the context (no clientNumber filter) so it's the highest-value paginate; the other five are per-client-bounded so risk is lower per-call but shape consistency still wins. Severity "medium" is right — not blocking, but a meaningful surface-uniformity defect for the LLM consumer.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Retrofit six tools with Pagination.Page<T>, mirroring the F13 pattern from ClientsTools/TablesTools. Concrete plan (all sim-actionable, no Windows required):

1) Add `int? limit = null, int? offset = null` parameters to each method:
   - EFileTools.LacerteEfStatus (highest priority — no clientNumber filter, returns full eFilings across context)
   - DetailsTools.LacerteDetailRead (high — 2000+ row partnership returns realistic)
   - SubclientsTools.LacerteSubclientRead (medium — 100+ partner partnerships)
   - StatesTools.LacerteStateRead + LacerteStateSubclientRead (low — already filterable by stateAbbrev, but uniformity wins)
   - StatusTools.LacerteStatusRead (low — typically <10 rows but shape consistency)
   - FormsTools.LacerteFormsRead (medium — return can have 50+ forms)

2) Body shape, e.g. for EFileTools:
   ```csharp
   var rows = await _session.ReadEFStatus().ConfigureAwait(false);
   var page = Pagination.Page(rows, limit, offset);
   return new { 
       count = page.Total,                  // legacy v0.1.x compat
       efStatuses = page.Rows,              // legacy v0.1.x compat (renamed to rows in v0.2)
       rows = page.Rows, total = page.Total, 
       limit = page.Limit, offset = page.Offset, 
       hasMore = page.HasMore, nextOffset = page.NextOffset 
   };
   ```
   Keep legacy `count` + domain-named array (`efStatuses`/`subclients`/`forms`/etc.) additive for v0.1.x — same back-compat policy as F13. Add to F15 (the v0.2 cleanup task) so these legacy keys get removed in the same breaking-change window.

3) Update each tool's `[Description]` attribute to mention "Supports limit (default 100, max 1000) + offset for pagination; returns {rows, total, limit, offset, hasMore, nextOffset}."

4) Update ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md lines 62 (#44), 67-68 (#45), 73 (#46), 79 (#47), 85 (#49) to document the paginated envelope, mirroring the language already in #42/#43. Add a uniform-contract assertion: "Every `lacerte_*_read` / `lacerte_*_list` tool returns the six pagination fields plus an additive legacy `count` through v0.1.x."

5) Tests: extend the existing 6 pagination tests pattern from F13 — for each tool, assert (a) default unbounded read returns full rows + correct total/hasMore=false, (b) limit=2 returns exactly 2 rows + hasMore=true + nextOffset=2, (c) offset past total returns empty rows + hasMore=false. Roughly 18 new test rows total. Existing parity tests in RoundTripTests.cs must keep reading via `count` to confirm back-compat.

6) Update F13's Todo.md entry to reference this retrofit, OR add a new F16 cross-cutting follow-up item describing "Pagination retrofit for remaining 6 read tools" so the audit trail is intact.

Skip the "expose Series/Code filter on detail_read" half of the original finding's recommendation — that's a separate finding worth its own task, and pagination alone is sufficient to unblock the 2000-detail-row case.

title: Idempotency cache eviction is O(n log n) per call at cap; no concurrent eviction safety
description: When _idempotencyCache.Count > 10,000, StoreIdempotent runs (a) a full foreach over all entries checking CreatedAt against cutoff, and (b) if still over cap, _idempotencyCache.OrderBy(kv => kv.Value.CreatedAt).FirstOrDefault() — that's an O(n log n) sort over 10k entries on the hot write path. Worse, this runs under the per-KEY semaphore but NOT a global eviction lock, so N concurrent writes to N different keys at-or-above the cap each independently sort the dictionary, each independently TryRemove the oldest entry, and the eviction becomes a thundering herd. Under sustained load right at cap this burns CPU and may evict more than intended (every concurrent writer drops a different 'oldest' candidate). The TTL pre-pass mitigates by typically dropping many entries at once, but a workload of unique keys all within the 24h window hits the OrderBy path repeatedly.
recommendation: Replace the OrderBy/TryRemove pattern with a bounded-FIFO structure: either (a) track insertion order in a ConcurrentQueue<string> of keys and evict head-batch when over cap, or (b) batch-evict (drop oldest 10% in one pass under a dedicated eviction lock so concurrent calls collapse to one). At minimum, gate the eviction block with `if (Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _evicting, 1, 0) == 0) { try {...} finally { Volatile.Write(ref _evicting, 0); } }` so only one writer sorts at a time. Also consider that batch-evicting in chunks (say 100 oldest) means a write at the cap pays the sort cost once per 100 writes instead of every write.
rationale: P14-013 added the cap; P14-064 confirmed it; neither finding considered eviction concurrency. For a long-running server that's the steady-state hot path once 10k unique idempotency keys accumulate (~3-4 days of moderate write traffic). The OrderBy pattern is exactly the kind of 'works in tests, dies under load' regression that an audit focused on test correctness wouldn't catch.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified by reading LacerteSessionManager.cs:1311-1395 and audit-findings.json. The code is exactly as described: StoreIdempotent (1364-1396) runs an O(n) foreach over the whole cache to drop expired entries, then if still over cap runs `_idempotencyCache.OrderBy(kv => kv.Value.CreatedAt)` — a full O(n log n) sort of ~10k entries on the hot write path. The eviction block runs INSIDE ExecuteWithIdempotencyLock (1317-1334), which is a PER-KEY SemaphoreSlim — concurrent writes to N different keys are NOT mutually excluded from each other's eviction passes, so the thundering-herd concern is real. The per-key semaphore design is documented at lines 1311-1316 ("per-key SemaphoreSlim") confirming there is no global eviction lock.

Phase-14 prior work: P14-013 (id at line 285 of audit-findings.json) introduced the cap with the exact OrderBy pattern in its refinedRecommendation ("scan and TryRemove all entries older than the TTL, and if still over cap, remove the oldest N by CreatedAt"). P14-064 (line 1407) confirmed it. Neither task addressed (a) eviction concurrency under per-key locking, nor (b) the O(n log n) per-call sort cost, nor (c) batch eviction to amortize. The current code comment at line 1372 even reads "Single LINQ scan over ~10k entries is fine for the cold path" — but the cold-path assumption breaks the moment the cache stabilizes at cap (then EVERY write hits the eviction block, not just an occasional one).

Severity calibration: For a single-operator stdio MCP (per CLAUDE.md "Personal tool"), concurrent same-millisecond writes from the LLM client are rare, and reaching 10k unique keys takes days. So this is hardening, not a live bug. But the fix is small, fully sim-actionable off-Windows, and prevents a real "works in tests, dies under load" regression. Severity medium (matches the finder).

Implementation cost is low: batch-evict 10% (1000 entries) per OrderBy pass amortizes the sort cost over 1000 writes, AND gating with `Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref _evicting, 1, 0)` collapses concurrent evictors to one. Two sim-only xUnit tests cover it: (a) stuff 11k entries, assert count drops to ~9k after one over-cap write, (b) fire N=50 concurrent over-cap writes with unique keys, assert final count is bounded (no over-eviction).

title: EditionDetection cached as 'Unavailable' forever on first transient probe failure
description: P14-061 made the edition probe cache-once-on-failure to honor the docstring contract 'never re-probed for the lifetime of the process'. The implementation sets _edition = EditionInfo('Unavailable', 'Unavailable', 'Unavailable') on ANY exception (BridgeUnavailable, transient COMException, RPC_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE, etc.) and never tries again. For a long-running server this means: (1) if the first SessionStatus() call happens during a brief Lacerte service hiccup or COM apartment startup race, the edition shows 'Unavailable' for the rest of the process life even after Lacerte recovers, (2) re-running Register() to refresh the 24h auth ticket does not refresh the edition cache, (3) if an operator updates Lacerte mid-session and re-registers, the cached value remains stale, and (4) AutoReconnect's retry logic is bypassed because Probe is called synchronously without retry wrapping.
recommendation: Distinguish permanent-unavailable (BridgeUnavailable with reason 'Live edition probe not yet implemented' — that's a Phase-9 code gap that won't change without a deployment) from transient-unavailable (COMException with a known transient HRESULT). Cache permanent failures forever; for transient failures, cache for a TTL (say 5 minutes) and retry on the next SessionStatus call. Alternatively, clear _edition in Register() so any successful re-registration re-probes the edition triple. Wrap the actual Probe() call with AutoReconnect.WithRetrySync so transient COM hiccups don't poison the cache.
rationale: P14-061 was added to fix a real bug (the cache was missing the throw path), but the fix overcorrected: 'cache the attempt forever' is wrong for transient errors. SessionStatus is one of the primary operator-facing diagnostic tools; baking 'Unavailable' into it for the full process lifetime over a 5ms RPC blip is a poor lifecycle behavior.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading LacerteSessionManager.cs lines 311-349, EditionDetection.cs, Register() lines 186-256, and the Phase-14 task list. P14-061's fix indeed catches ALL exceptions (line 331-346) and bakes the "Unavailable" sentinel into _edition for the process lifetime with no distinction between (a) permanent unavailability (the current Phase-9 stub that always throws BridgeUnavailable with "Live edition probe not yet implemented") and (b) transient COM/RPC failures that will appear once Phase 9 wires the real probe. Confirmed via Grep that Register() never clears _edition — so a re-register after the 24h auth window (or after an operator restarts the Lacerte service mid-session) does NOT refresh the edition triple. Confirmed Probe is called directly without AutoReconnect.WithRetrySync wrapping (Register() IS wrapped at line 223, but the edition path is not). The cached-Unavailable behavior in SessionStatus is then silently surfaced because SessionStatus's outer catch at line 280 also coerces edition probe failures to null — but with P14-061 the inner Unavailable triple is returned directly, so SessionStatus surfaces stale "Unavailable" even after Lacerte recovers. P14-061 and P14-056 are the only Phase-14 tasks touching this code; neither distinguishes transient vs permanent nor invalidates on Register(). The current symptom is latent today (sim Probe never throws; live Probe is always permanent until Phase 9), but the finding is correct that the fix overshoots and will hurt the moment Phase 9 wires real late-bound COM reads. Medium severity is fair — operator-facing diagnostic (lacerte_session_status) is the only consumer. The simplest valuable fix today is to clear _edition in Register() so a re-register naturally refreshes the cache; the transient-vs-permanent TTL split is a Phase-9-or-later concern and would be premature now.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Two minimal sim-testable fixes; defer the TTL/transient classification to Phase 9 when real COMExceptions can actually be thrown.

(1) Clear the edition cache in Register() — add `lock (_editionLock) { _edition = null; }` at the top of Register() (before the WireLog wrapper). This means any successful re-registration (24h auth refresh, mid-session Lacerte restart, operator-triggered re-register after a service hiccup) naturally re-probes the edition. Document the invariant in the _edition field comment: "Cleared on Register() so re-auth refreshes the triple; otherwise one-shot per registration."

(2) Add a unit test in LacerteSessionManagerTests.cs using a fake ILacerteBridge that records Probe-equivalent call count: (a) bridge throws on first Probe → SessionStatus returns Unavailable triple, (b) call Register() (which succeeds), (c) bridge configured to succeed on next Probe → second SessionStatus returns the real triple. Asserts Probe was invoked exactly twice across the two SessionStatus calls. Today this can be smoke-tested by having the test inject a bridge via the internal test ctor.

Explicitly NOT in scope right now: (a) wrapping Probe in AutoReconnect.WithRetrySync — Phase 9 should do this when it wires the real late-bound reads, not in advance against a stub that only throws BridgeUnavailable; (b) transient-vs-permanent HRESULT classification — same reasoning, premature without a real COM call to classify against. File a Phase-9 follow-up note in DECISIONS.md so this isn't lost: "When EditionDetection.Probe gains real COM reads (Phase 9), wrap in AutoReconnect.WithRetrySync and distinguish RPC_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE (transient, TTL-cache) from BridgeUnavailable (permanent, lifetime-cache)."

title: No proactive 24h-auth-expiry probe; operator gets raw NotSignedIn instead of 9100 SessionExpired
description: The session manager knows ExpiresAt (set on Register at line 230/246) and SessionStatus correctly computes MinutesUntilExpiry. SyntheticStatusCodes 9100 'SessionExpired' is defined with a friendly remediation message ('Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate'). But NO write/read chokepoint checks `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow > ExpiresAt` before dispatching the wire call. The flow today is reactive: a tool call after 24h hits the bridge, the SDK returns TAPIStatus NotSignedIn (203), the operator sees a raw integer status. The synthetic 9100 with its operator-friendly message is never emitted. For a long-running session the friendly synthetic code is the entire point — it tells the operator what to DO rather than handing them a TAPIStatus to decode.
recommendation: Add a private bool IsAuthExpired() helper that returns ExpiresAt.HasValue && DateTimeOffset.UtcNow >= ExpiresAt.Value, and call it inside RequireContext (or as a separate Throw-if-expired helper) at the top of every write/read chokepoint. On true, throw new LacerteSDKError(SyntheticStatusCodes.SessionExpired, ctx) — proactive 9100 instead of reactive 203. The check is essentially free (one DateTimeOffset comparison) and turns the cliff-edge 24h failure into a clean structured error with the documented remediation.
rationale: The 9100 code, the +24h ExpiresAt stamp, and the SessionStatus MinutesUntilExpiry computation all exist and are consistent with the operator-facing UX in agent 02 §6 — but nothing wires them together. The audit-findings.json shows no Phase-14 task addressed the proactive expiry probe. The reviewer asked specifically: 'when SetContext is called after expiry, does the response give a clear remediation? Is there a probe before each call or only reactive?' The current answer is 'reactive only.'

verdict.reasoning:
Verified directly. Real issue: LacerteSessionManager.ExpiresAt is set on Register (lines 230/246) and read by SessionStatus (lines 265-268) for the MinutesUntilExpiry display, but NOTHING in the chokepoints consults it. RequireContext (line 980-988) only null-checks Context — no expiry probe. AutoReconnect.cs:137 explicitly comments that NotSignedIn propagates unchanged ("need re-auth, not retry"). In sim, SimulationStore has an _sessionExpired latch but it's env-var-toggled (LACERTE_SIM_EXPIRED=1), NOT wall-clock driven, so a sim session left running past +24h would never trigger any expired check either. Both modes are reactive-only.

One factual inaccuracy in the finding: it references SyntheticStatusCodes.SessionExpired at code 9100 — that constant does not exist. The actual auth-lifecycle codes are LoginExpired=9007 (validation range, with the operator-friendly StatusInfo message "Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate (consent is one-time; only the sign-in needs refresh).") and ReAuthRequired=9101 (in the 9100 auth-lifecycle range). 9100 itself is unused. The underlying defect — no proactive probe, operator gets raw 203 instead of a friendly synthetic code — is fully valid, but the recommendation must use the right constant.

NOT a Phase-14 duplicate: searched audit-findings.json for SessionExpired/9100/IsAuthExpired/proactive-expir/expiry-probe/24h-auth (case insensitive) and Todo.md Phase 14 — the only related Phase-14 work is P14-013 (idempotency cache TTL, different concern) and a README troubleshooting entry that *mentions* the 24h expiry symptom but does not add a code-level probe. The Sim's existing _sessionExpired latch is env-only and confirms nothing was wired to clock time.

Fully actionable off-Windows: pure in-process check on a DateTimeOffset comparison, no Lacerte SDK, no Windows. Test seam: the existing test-only ctor (line 166) can be used; need a small additional hook to inject a fake clock OR an internal setter for ExpiresAt so a test can pre-stamp it in the past. Both are one-line additions.

Useful: in a 24h+ session every subsequent write-tool call returns an opaque integer (203 in live, or in sim today: nothing at all because the wall-clock check doesn't exist) with no remediation hint. The 9007 synthetic code's documented Remediation field ("Run lacerte_register to re-authenticate") is the entire DX point. Fix is ~15 lines + a focused test. Not bikeshedding.

title: FieldAccessMap shards loaded once, never invalidated; FieldAccessDumper output not picked up until process restart
description: _moduleCache and _overlayCache are ConcurrentDictionary<...> populated lazily via GetOrAdd; entries are never invalidated except by the test-only ResetCacheForTests(). The intended Phase-13 operator workflow is: run LacertMCP.FieldAccessDumper.exe to introspect live SDK and write a fresh Schema/FieldAccessMap/base/individual.json, then exercise tools. With the MCP server running long-lived (the spec scenario), the new JSON file is on disk but the in-process cache still holds the empty / stale map from the first AssertWritable. Writes that should now succeed continue to throw UnknownFieldAccess (9012) until process restart. Worse: the malformed-JSON degrade-to-empty path (lines 318-324) caches an empty sentinel; if the operator fixes the typo while the server runs, the fix is invisible.
recommendation: Either (a) add a public ReloadCaches() method exposed via a CLI command / MCP tool ('lacerte_reload_schema') that calls _moduleCache.Clear() + _overlayCache.Clear(), or (b) attach a FileSystemWatcher to SchemaRoot() that invalidates the cache entry for the modified file. Option (a) is cheaper and more explicit (no surprise reloads mid-tool). Document the limitation in README's troubleshooting section so operators know dumper output requires a server restart OR the reload command.
rationale: The Phase-13 dumper exists explicitly to populate the access map, and the README points operators at it as the supported path for filling Unknown entries. Without a cache-invalidation path, the dumper workflow requires a server bounce — which kills any in-flight Intuit 24h auth ticket and forces a re-register dance. Reviewer asked: 'Loading the field-access shards: re-loaded per call or cached? Stale-cache invalidation if a JSON file changes on disk?' — both questions have 'no' answers today.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified at C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Server/Schema/FieldAccessMapLoader.cs:50-54 (caches) and lines 237-326 (GetOrAdd factories). Both `_moduleCache` and `_overlayCache` are populated lazily and only ever cleared by the `internal` `ResetCacheForTests()` (line 338) — there is no public/CLI/MCP reload path. The malformed-JSON cache-an-empty-sentinel behavior is also confirmed at lines 318-324 (`catch (JsonException)` → empty TaxYearOverlay cached forever).

The Phase-13 dumper workflow that materializes the gap is documented at HANDOFF.md:47 — operators are explicitly directed to run `LacertMCP.FieldAccessDumper.exe` against a long-lived setup. With the MCP server running, the dumper writes a fresh `Schema/FieldAccessMap/base/individual.json` to disk, but the in-process cache still holds the `{}` v1 stub loaded at first `AssertWritable`. Every subsequent write returns synthetic 9012 UnknownFieldAccess until the operator restarts the server — which per project context invalidates the Intuit 24h auth ticket and forces a re-register dance.

Searched all 71 Phase-14 tasks in Todo.md (P14-001..071) and audit-findings.json verdicts for keywords `reload`, `invalidat`, `FileSystemWatcher`, `ResetCache`, `hot-reload`, `cache.*clear`: zero matches. Phase 14 touched FieldAccessMapLoader at P14-020 (Modules dedup), P14-024 (test coverage), P14-029 (case-sensitivity), P14-032 (per-year overlay semantic doc), P14-063 (string allocation) — none address cache lifecycle. The dumper itself (F5) shipped but with no story for getting its output into a running server. This is a genuine new gap.

Fully actionable off-Windows: it's pure in-process C# (promote `ResetCacheForTests` to a public `ReloadCaches()`, wire a CLI verb + MCP tool, add a regression test using the temp Schema dir pattern already used by FieldAccessMapCoverageTests). No Lacerte SDK or Windows install required.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Implement option (a) — explicit reload, skip the FileSystemWatcher path (a watcher would reload mid-tool, fight the dumper's multi-file rewrite, and create non-deterministic test behavior; the docstring at lines 32-38 already commits to single-load semantics as a feature). Concretely:

1. **FieldAccessMapLoader.cs** — Promote `ResetCacheForTests` to a documented public API. Rename to `ReloadCaches()`, keep the body (`_moduleCache.Clear(); _overlayCache.Clear();`), and have `ResetCacheForTests` call it. Return a small struct `(int modulesEvicted, int overlaysEvicted)` so callers can report back.

2. **CLI** — Add `lacerte-mcp field-access reload` next to the existing `set/list/discover` verbs in `src/LacertMCP.Cli/Commands/FieldAccessCommand.cs`. Since the CLI runs out-of-process, this verb has no in-process effect on a running server; document it as a no-op-from-CLI that prints "run via MCP tool `lacerte_reload_schema` to affect the running server" — OR just skip the CLI verb and only ship the MCP tool. The latter is cleaner.

3. **MCP tool** — Add `lacerte_reload_schema` to `src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/MetadataTools.cs` (the existing home for `lacerte_field_access_map`). Wrap in `WrapToolHandler.Run`, no session needed, returns `{ "modulesEvicted": N, "overlaysEvicted": M, "schemaRoot": "<path>" }`. Add a `[Description]` that explicitly mentions the FieldAccessDumper workflow: "Call after running LacertMCP.FieldAccessDumper.exe so the new shards take effect without restarting the server (which would invalidate the Intuit 24h auth ticket)."

4. **Tests** — Add `FieldAccessMapLoaderReloadTests.cs`: (a) write empty shard to temp dir → `GetFieldAccess` returns Unknown; (b) rewrite shard with a real entry on disk; (c) assert `GetFieldAccess` still returns the cached Unknown (proves the bug); (d) call `ReloadCaches()`; (e) assert it now returns the new entry. Also add the malformed-then-fixed variant: cache an empty sentinel from a bad JSON, fix the file, reload, assert recovery. Use `[Collection("AccessMapMutation")]` per the existing race-mitigation pattern from Todo task #55.

5. **README + HANDOFF** — Add a Troubleshooting bullet: "If the FieldAccessDumper produced fresh shards but writes still return 9012 UnknownFieldAccess, call the `lacerte_reload_schema` MCP tool — restarting the server is unnecessary and will invalidate the 24h auth ticket." HANDOFF step #47 should be updated to mention the reload step right after the dumper invocation.

title: OdbcConnection cached forever; no detection or recovery from server-side disconnect
description: EnsureOpen opens an OdbcConnection on first Query and reuses it for the life of the reader. The only re-open path is `if (_connection.State != ConnectionState.Open)` — but a server-side disconnect (DBF on a network share that became unreachable, DSN reconfigured, ODBC driver process died) doesn't always flip State to Closed. The connection stays in Open while the next ExecuteReader throws OdbcException with HY000 / 08S01 / 08003. OdbcErrorMapper translates the exception but does NOT dispose+null _connection, so every subsequent Query throws the same error against the same dead connection until Dispose() is called manually. AutoReconnect.WithRetry is NEVER applied to the ODBC path (it wraps COM calls only via WithRetrySync). For a long-running server that survives a midnight DSN refresh or a network blip, ODBC reads become permanently broken without a process restart.
recommendation: Wrap the OdbcException catch in LacerteDsnReader.Query: when the OdbcException SqlState indicates a connection-level failure (08S01 communication-link failure, 08003 connection-not-open, HY000 generic — or check ex.Errors[0].SQLState), dispose _connection and null it before the throw so the NEXT Query re-opens fresh. Optionally add AutoReconnect-style retry once with the reopened connection. Add an explicit Ping() helper that runs a cheap `SELECT 1` and dispose+null on failure; can be called by lacerte_session_status to surface ODBC health.
rationale: The class docstring claims 'connection is opened lazily on the first query and reused for subsequent queries; Dispose closes the connection' — but for a long-running server 'reuse forever' without disconnect recovery is broken. P14-021 (the audit-findings entry that deleted ConnectionPool.cs) leaned on the OS provider's pool but didn't address the per-reader connection lifecycle. Reviewer's question 'when is the underlying OdbcConnection closed? If kept open, what about a server-side disconnect?' has no answer in the current code.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by direct read of LacerteDsnReader.cs (lines 102-118 + 124-135) and Grep across the codebase. The OdbcException catch in Query() maps via OdbcErrorMapper and rethrows without ever disposing/nulling _connection. EnsureOpen only re-opens when State != Open, which doesn't fire for many server-side disconnects (08S01 communication-link failure, 08003 connection-not-open, HY000 generic — exactly the codes OdbcErrorMapper.MapSqlState already buckets as DBFNotAccessable on lines 76-80). A second Grep confirms LacerteDsnReader.cs has zero references to AutoReconnect/WithRetry — only LacerteSessionManager wraps the _bridge COM calls in WithRetry. Not a Phase-14 duplicate: P14-021 (EfStatusJoin SELECT list), P14-022 (row-number resolution), P14-060 (typed _odbc field), P14-066 (deleted ConnectionPool), P14-023 (AutoReconnect HRESULT test coverage) are the closest but none address EnsureOpen's recovery after a server-side disconnect. The ODBC reader is still un-wired at the session manager (line 68: LacerteDsnReader? _odbc with CS0649 warning suppression and a "null until first ODBC read" comment), so the bug is forward-looking — it will activate the instant Phase-9 ODBC wire-up lands. Useful because a single network blip during overnight running would otherwise need a process restart. Sim-actionable: the fix is pure C# in LacerteDsnReader.Query plus a Ping() helper; tests can use a small adapter seam (extract IDbCommand/IDbConnection factory, inject a throwing fake) without any Windows/ODBC dependency. One nuance worth tightening in the recommendation: a SELECT 1 ping won't work against the Lacerte DBF ODBC driver (no virtual rowset), so the health probe should run a cheap real query.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Two targeted changes in src/LacertMCP.Server/Odbc/LacerteDsnReader.cs (sim-only, no Windows needed): (1) In the catch (OdbcException ex) block at lines 112-118, before rethrowing, call a new private TryRecycleConnectionOnFatal(ex) that inspects ex.Errors[0]?.SQLState (defensive null guard) and disposes+nulls _connection when the state starts with "08" OR equals "IM002" OR starts with "HY" — i.e. exactly the set OdbcErrorMapper.MapSqlState already classifies as DBFNotAccessable/CodeBaseError on lines 76-80 and 100-105. Reuse that classification rather than inlining a parallel whitelist; expose a small `OdbcErrorMapper.IsConnectionFatal(string sqlState)` predicate so the two sites can't drift. This guarantees the next Query() goes through EnsureOpen()'s `_connection == null` branch and opens fresh. Do NOT add inline retry here — keep the Query throw behavior unchanged; the session manager owns the policy and can opt into a single sim-friendly AutoReconnect.WithRetrySync wrapper around its Odbc.Query callsites once Phase-9 wires _odbc through ListClients/ReadTableCore/etc. (2) Add a public bool Ping() helper that runs a cheap, schema-aware probe — NOT `SELECT 1` (the Lacerte DBF driver has no virtual rowset). Use `SELECT TOP 1 C1_0 FROM [DATA1-Client Info]` since DATA1 is universally present per the spec; catch OdbcException, route through the same TryRecycleConnectionOnFatal, and return false. Wire Ping() into SessionTools.LacerteSessionStatus so the operator can see ODBC health and trigger recycle before a tool call hangs. Tests (off-Windows): extract a tiny `Func<string, IDbConnection>` factory seam in LacerteDsnReader's ctor (default `s => new OdbcConnection(s)`); inject a fake connection whose CreateCommand returns a fake command that throws an OdbcException-shaped exception with a chosen SQLState. Assert (a) first Query throws LacerteSDKError DBFNotAccessable AND a follow-up assertion that _connection is now null via reflection or a `bool HasOpenConnection { get; }` test-only property; (b) a subsequent Query opens a fresh connection (the factory is called a second time); (c) Ping() returns false on connection-fatal exceptions and true on a successful read; (d) non-connection SQLState (e.g. 42S02 table not found) does NOT recycle the connection. ~4 facts, all sim-only. Skip the AutoReconnect.WithRetry wrapping here — it belongs in LacerteSessionManager when it actually calls _odbc, not inside the reader.

title: Program.cs has no graceful shutdown — ODBC/COM/idempotency leak on SIGTERM
description: Program.Main does `await builder.Build().RunAsync()` with no hosted-service registration, no IHostApplicationLifetime stop hook, and no Console.CancelKeyPress / AppDomain.ProcessExit handler. LacerteSessionManager is registered as a singleton and IS IDisposable (releases _bridge as IDisposable, disposes _odbc and every _idempotencyLocks SemaphoreSlim), but Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting only invokes IDisposable on the ServiceProvider when the host stops gracefully — if the MCP client (Claude Desktop) just kills the stdio pipe, RunAsync may return abruptly and the singleton may never dispose. WireLog has its own ProcessExit hook (good) but the session manager does not. In live mode this means a Ctrl+C / pipe-close leaves the COM ref unreleased and the 24h Intuit auth ticket pinned.
recommendation: Two cheap, additive changes: (1) Add `Console.CancelKeyPress += (_,e) => { e.Cancel = true; host.StopAsync(); };` after `var host = builder.Build();` so Ctrl+C drains gracefully. (2) Register a hosted service or use `host.Services.GetRequiredService<IHostApplicationLifetime>().ApplicationStopping.Register(...)` to dispose the singleton explicitly. (3) Also add an `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.ProcessExit` handler that calls _bridge.Dispose() as a last-resort net for the abrupt-kill case. Same pattern WireLog already uses for its StreamWriter cache — copy it.
rationale: Round-1 covered WireLog StreamWriter lifecycle and COM RCW release in Bridge methods, but Program-level shutdown wiring (the layer that calls Dispose at all) was not in scope. Without this, the COM/ODBC release paths the round-1 fixes added only run on clean exit, not on pipe-close — exactly the case a server hosted by Claude Desktop hits.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by direct read of Program.cs (lines 18-44), LacerteSessionManager.cs (line 47 IDisposable + line 1455-1466 real Dispose body that releases _bridge, _odbc, and every idempotency SemaphoreSlim), WireLog.cs (line 503 ProcessExit hook confirms the finding's claim that WireLog already has this pattern), and a full grep of audit-findings.json. No Phase-14 task touched Program.cs lifecycle — the only Program.cs references in audit-findings.json are: (a) CLAUDE.md doc-update entry naming the file, (b) README prompts section naming the file, (c) ARCHITECTURE.md Bridge-row update, (d) CLI Program.cs (different file under LacertMCP.Cli), and (e) UpdateReturnTools registration mention. None added shutdown wiring. The Todo.md Phase-14 block (P14-001..P14-071) contains nothing for Program.cs server-side lifecycle.\n\nThe finding is technically correct but the recommendation slightly over-engineers. The core bug is that `await builder.Build().RunAsync()` never wraps the Host in `using` / `await using`, so the IHost (and its ServiceProvider, and therefore the LacerteSessionManager singleton) is never disposed even on a clean graceful exit. Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting's default ConsoleLifetime DOES already register Console.CancelKeyPress and AppDomain.ProcessExit handlers that call StopAsync — that part the finding gets slightly wrong (the suggested CancelKeyPress handler is largely redundant). The real gap is the missing host disposal after RunAsync returns. On abrupt SIGKILL/pipe-kill no managed code can run regardless, so a ProcessExit handler in Program.cs only helps the narrow \"process exits but RunAsync returned without ConsoleLifetime firing\" window — still cheap to add as belt-and-suspenders since LacerteSessionManager is a singleton with real native handles (COM RCW once Phase 9 lands, ODBC pool, semaphores). Sim-only, in-session fix: 2-5 lines in one file.

title: Six read tools return unbounded result sets — MCP message-size footgun
file: src/LacertMCP.Server/Tools/DetailsTools.cs + EFileTools.cs + SubclientsTools.cs + StatesTools.cs + FormsTools.cs + StatusTools.cs + MetadataTools.cs
line: DetailsTools.cs:62-78 / EFileTools.cs:21-29 / SubclientsTools.cs:21-34 / StatesTools.cs:20-52 / FormsTools.cs:20-33 / StatusTools.cs:21-34 / MetadataTools.cs:121-165
description: Round-1 P14-014 paginated ClientsTools and TablesTools, but LacerteDetailRead, LacerteEfStatus, LacerteStateRead, LacerteStateSubclientRead, LacerteFormsRead, LacerteSubclientRead, LacerteStatusRead, and LacerteReturnCodes still return the full unfiltered result set with no limit/offset/cursor. A partnership with 200 partners, a high-volume practice's EF roster (200+ filings per module-year), or an active client's detail file (hundreds of W-2/1099/Sch-C rows) can easily push past 1 MB of JSON. MCP stdio frames are length-prefixed JSON-RPC and most clients impose a per-message cap (Claude Desktop's is in the low MBs); even when it works, the unbounded responses defeat the entire pagination contract the round-1 fix established. LacerteReturnCodes also dumps the full 28-code TAPIStatus table + synthetic codes every call — small today but grows without bound.
recommendation: Apply the same Pagination.Page<T> wrapper used in TablesTools/ClientsTools to the seven affected tools. Add `int limit = 100, int offset = 0` parameters with the same [Description] phrasing TablesTools uses. Returns become `{ rows, total, limit, offset, hasMore, nextOffset, ... }`. Keep the legacy top-level array key for v0.1 back-compat (matches the existing v0.1 pattern). EFStatus + Detail are the highest-priority of the set because detail rows are unbounded by design (per-client store).
rationale: MCP pagination is now a project convention (round-1 P14-014 landed it as the canonical shape). Leaving 7 of ~14 read tools without pagination is an inconsistent surface for the LLM AND a real wire-size risk in production. Round-1 only fixed the two tools the brief named — the rest were missed.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading all seven cited tool files plus ClientsTools.cs and TablesTools.cs for the canonical pagination shape, plus Pagination.cs, plus a full sweep of audit-findings.json and Todo.md Phase-14 section. Findings: (1) DetailsTools.LacerteDetailRead (line 65-78), EFileTools.LacerteEfStatus (21-28), SubclientsTools.LacerteSubclientRead (21-34), StatesTools.LacerteStateRead + LacerteStateSubclientRead (20-52), FormsTools.LacerteFormsRead (20-33), StatusTools.LacerteStatusRead (21-34) all return `new { count, rows }` with zero limit/offset parameters — the full unfiltered result from the session manager. (2) P14-014 verified to be ClientsTools-only; no other Phase-14 task touched pagination on these tools. Todo.md confirms only ListClients (P14-014) was paginated in the recent wave; TablesTools was paginated earlier (per task #77 / Phase 11 comment in Pagination.cs). (3) Realistic wire-size risk is genuine for EFStatus (module-wide join, no client filter) and Detail (per-client but row-unbounded by design — every W-2/1099/dependent/partner emits one row); Subclients/States/StateSubclients are per-client but partnership returns with 100+ partners × 50 states can plausibly emit thousands of rows. (4) Forms/Status per-client rarely exceed 30 rows in real returns — pagination there is consistency-driven, not size-driven. (5) The finding overreaches by listing MetadataTools.LacerteReturnCodes (~38 fixed entries, bounded) and LacerteFieldAccessMap (bounded by an explicit 26-probe + 3-suffix loop on lines 85-107) — those don't merit pagination. (6) Implementation is mechanical: each affected tool already has the wire pattern set by TablesTools.cs:30-52 (Pagination.Page<T> + dual-shape legacy compat), and tests follow PaginationTests.cs. Pure off-Windows sim-only work, no COM/ODBC/Windows dependency. Confidence high; refining the recommendation to drop the two MetadataTools entries and rank by realistic risk.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Apply Pagination.Page<T> to six tools, ranked by realistic wire-size risk; SKIP MetadataTools (both methods bounded by static or fixed-probe enumeration). Per-tool work mirrors the TablesTools.cs:30-52 pattern exactly — add `int limit = 100, int offset = 0` parameters with TablesTools' [Description] phrasing, wrap the session result via `Pagination.Pagination.Page(rows, limit, offset)`, and keep the legacy top-level collection key (`subclients`/`states`/`forms`/`statuses`/`rows`/`efStatuses`) + `count` for v0.1 back-compat alongside the new `rows/total/limit/offset/hasMore/nextOffset` fields (the v0.1→v0.2 deprecation note is already in DECISIONS.md per P14-037). Priority order: (1) EFileTools.LacerteEfStatus — HIGHEST: module-wide join with no client filter, busy practice can emit 200+ rows of 6-key dicts; (2) DetailsTools.LacerteDetailRead — HIGH: per-client store unbounded by design (every W-2/1099/dependent/partner row); (3) SubclientsTools.LacerteSubclientRead — MEDIUM: partnership/S-corp returns scale with partner/shareholder count; (4) StatesTools.LacerteStateRead + LacerteStateSubclientRead — MEDIUM: scales with state count × subclient count for multistate partnerships; (5) FormsTools.LacerteFormsRead + StatusTools.LacerteStatusRead — LOW (consistency-only): rarely exceed 30 rows in practice but worth doing in the same sweep so the LLM sees one paginated shape across all read tools. Tests: extend the existing PaginationTests pattern with one round-trip per tool asserting (a) default limit=100, (b) hasMore=true when total>limit, (c) legacy collection key still present. Update the README tool table to flag the new pagination params. Skip MetadataTools entirely: LacerteReturnCodes is bounded by the static StatusCodes.StatusTable + SyntheticStatusCodes.StatusTable (~38 entries combined); LacerteFieldAccessMap is bounded by the explicit 26-probe + 3-suffix loop at MetadataTools.cs:85-107. Add a one-line ADR addition to DECISIONS.md's pagination entry noting "all DATA-row read tools (Clients/Tables/Subclients/States/StateSubclients/Status/Forms/Details/EFStatus) implement the paginated envelope; pure-metadata tools (ReturnCodes, FieldAccessMap) are bounded by static tables and intentionally do not paginate."

title: WrapToolHandler error envelope is undocumented — README/ARCHITECTURE never specify the shape
description: Every tool returns a serialized envelope: `{success:true, result:{...}}` on success, `{success:false, statusCode, statusName, severity, userMessage, remediation, context}` on error. This is a load-bearing contract — the LLM is supposed to parse `success` and act on `remediation` — but neither README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, nor the Lacerte_MCP_Structure_Spec.md document the envelope shape. A model calling the server has to infer it from the first error response. Worse, this envelope nests inside MCP's own ToolResult content blocks; clients may unwrap differently. Round-1 P14-026 fixed the misleading `api` field but did NOT add an envelope contract anywhere operator- or model-facing.
recommendation: Add a `## Tool Response Envelope` section to README.md after the Tools table, with two example JSON blobs (success and error) and a description of every field. Cite WrapToolHandler.cs as the canonical implementation. Also add the success/error shape to ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md so any future tool that bypasses WrapToolHandler can be flagged in review. Cross-link from WorkflowPrompts.cs descriptions so the prompts mention `surface the structured statusCode + userMessage + remediation from the tool response` (which they already do — but the operator reading the README has no reference for what those fields are).
rationale: Round-1's audit only flagged the `api` field drift (P14-026); the broader envelope contract was treated as implicit. With WrapToolHandler now also doing redaction on error envelopes (PII in `context` dicts), the shape is even more load-bearing and deserves a documented schema.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by reading README.md (full file), ARCHITECTURE.md (lines 80, 128-153), ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md (lines 33, 100), WrapToolHandler.cs, and grepping the entire audit-findings.json + Todo.md Phase 14. The finding is factually accurate about README: grep for envelope/wraptoolhandler/success.result/response shape returns ZERO hits in README.md. An operator/LLM landing on the README sees the Tools table at line 122 and the env-var table but nothing about response shape. However, the finding overreaches when claiming ARCHITECTURE.md and Lacerte_MCP_Structure_Spec.md don't document it: ARCHITECTURE.md Invariant #9 (line 80) lists the full error field set verbatim `{ success: false, statusCode, statusName, severity, userMessage, remediation, context }` and the Tool Conventions section (line 128-153) shows the WrapToolHandler.Run pattern. ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md lines 33 and 100 already document both success and error envelopes precisely. So the documentation gap is narrower than the finding claims: it's a README-only gap, plus a missed opportunity to consolidate one canonical section with worked JSON examples. Not a duplicate of any Phase 14 item — P14-026 fixed the misleading `api` field in UpdateReturnTools' response, P14-014 added redaction to envelopes, and P14-022 retitled README/ACCEPTANCE for pagination, but no Phase 14 task adds a "Tool Response Envelope" README section. Refined recommendation tightens scope to README only and cites the already-correct ARCH/ACCEPTANCE docs to copy from, avoiding three redundant updates. Fix is pure doc work, off-Windows trivial, isUseful because an MCP client config in README without the envelope shape forces every consumer to reverse-engineer the contract from a first error response — and the contract IS load-bearing (WorkflowPrompts already tell the agent to surface statusCode + userMessage + remediation, which assumes the reader knows those fields exist).
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add a single `## Tool Response Envelope` section to README.md between the Tools tables (~line 154) and `## Prompts`. Three blocks: (1) success example `{"success": true, "result": {...tool-specific...}}` with one real example from `lacerte_client_list` (paginated rows); (2) error example `{"success": false, "statusCode": 9101, "statusName": "NotSignedIn", "severity": "error", "userMessage": "...", "remediation": "Run lacerte-mcp login...", "context": {}}`; (3) a one-liner field table (severity is `info|warning|error`, context is a free-form dict, both envelopes are post-redacted via WireLog). Cite `src/LacertMCP.Server/Errors/WrapToolHandler.cs` as the canonical implementation and link `ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA.md` lines 33/100 (which already specify the shape and should remain the spec — README is the operator-facing mirror). Do NOT duplicate into Lacerte_MCP_Structure_Spec.md (that file is the SDK source spec, not project response shape) or re-add to ARCHITECTURE.md (Invariant #9 already covers it). Add one cross-link from `WorkflowPrompts.cs` "surface the structured statusCode + userMessage + remediation" descriptions pointing to the new README section so the prompt copy is self-explanatory to the LLM consumer. Skip the ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA addition the original finding suggested — it's already there. Estimated 20 lines of README delta, 0 code changes, 0 tests.

title: Prompts never exercised end-to-end through an MCP host — only static methods are tested
description: WorkflowPromptsTests calls the static methods directly (`WorkflowPrompts.ClientIntake()`) and asserts on the returned GetPromptResult. It never stands up an MCP server, never sends `prompts/list` or `prompts/get` over JSON-RPC, and never verifies the SDK's auto-discovery (`WithPromptsFromAssembly()` in Program.cs:40) actually picks up the static class. If a future refactor removes [McpServerPromptType], drops the static modifier, or breaks the constructor (DI on prompts has subtle rules), the unit tests still pass but `prompts/list` would return empty over the wire and the brief's question 'has anyone driven them?' would be answered 'no'. Round-1 P14-015 added README docs for the prompts but did not add an end-to-end roundtrip test.
recommendation: Add one integration test that constructs an in-process MCP server with `AddMcpServer().WithPromptsFromAssembly(typeof(WorkflowPrompts).Assembly)`, then drives it via the SDK's in-process client (the ModelContextProtocol library ships a `McpClient` for this) issuing `prompts/list` (assert all 3 names present) and `prompts/get` for each with sample args (assert single user-role message). This catches the discovery seam, not just the body text. If the SDK doesn't expose a test client cheaply, fall back to invoking the prompt-resolution code path through `IMcpServer.GetPromptsAsync` from the DI container.
rationale: WorkflowPrompts and the SDK auto-discovery seam are unverified beyond the body string. The whole reason for WithPromptsFromAssembly is runtime discovery; testing the static method bypasses the only part that can break silently in production.

verdict.reasoning: Verified by direct inspection. WorkflowPromptsTests.cs (78 lines, all 6 facts) calls WorkflowPrompts.ClientIntake()/ReviewEfStatus()/BulkFieldUpdate() as plain static methods and asserts on the returned GetPromptResult. It never instantiates an MCP server, never exercises [McpServerPromptType]/[McpServerPrompt] reflection, never traverses WithPromptsFromAssembly() in Program.cs:40, and never sends prompts/list or prompts/get over JSON-RPC. A regression that drops [McpServerPromptType], renames the class out of the scanned assembly, or breaks SDK auto-discovery would leave all 6 unit tests green while prompts/list returns empty over the wire — exactly the silent-delist failure mode integration tests exist to catch. Phase 14 dedupe is clean: P14-015 (Todo.md:265) only added a README Prompts table, P14-034 only edited README+ARCHITECTURE.md, P14-036 added ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA rows. None added test coverage of the discovery seam. Grep across src/LacertMCP.Tests/ for StreamServerTransport / StreamClientTransport / McpClientFactory / ListPromptsAsync / CallToolAsync returns zero source hits — no in-process roundtrip test exists for ANY MCP surface (tools or prompts), so the finding is actually a representative of a wider gap. Actionable off-Windows: MCP SDK 0.3.0-preview.4 ships ModelContextProtocol.Server.StreamServerTransport (XML doc line 10533) and ModelContextProtocol.Protocol.StreamClientTransport (line 2984), both ctor(input Stream, output Stream, ...), reachable from netstandard2.0/net48. Pair them via two System.IO.Pipelines.Pipe instances (or two anonymous pipes); no Lacerte, no DSN, no Windows-only API. IMcpClient extensions expose ListPromptsAsync (XML doc confirmed) and the GetPrompt round-trip lives in the same extension set. One caveat about the original recommendation: the "fall back to IMcpServer.GetPromptsAsync from DI" suggestion is the wrong shape — assembly scanning happens at host build, not DI resolution, so that fallback wouldn't actually catch the discovery break. The StreamServer/Client pair is the correct cheap path.
verdict.refinedRecommendation:
Add ONE new test class at C:/Users/VR/Projects/LacertMCP/src/LacertMCP.Tests/Integration/McpDiscoveryRoundtripTests.cs that stands up an in-process MCP server and drives it through a real JSON-RPC pair. Implementation sketch (xUnit, async, net48-safe):

1) Build server via Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.Host.CreateApplicationBuilder, register AddMcpServer().WithPromptsFromAssembly(typeof(LacertMCP.Server.Prompts.WorkflowPrompts).Assembly).WithToolsFromAssembly(typeof(LacertMCP.Server.Tools.SessionTools).Assembly) — same call shape as Program.cs:36-40 minus WithStdioServerTransport. Override the transport: add a singleton ITransport bound to a ModelContextProtocol.Server.StreamServerTransport(serverIn, serverOut, "test", NullLoggerFactory.Instance) where serverIn/serverOut are the read/write halves of two System.IO.Pipelines.Pipe instances (or AnonymousPipeServerStream pairs). Also register LacerteSessionManager singleton (the prompts don't need it, but tools do — keeps the test reusable).

2) Construct an IMcpClient via new McpClient(new ModelContextProtocol.Protocol.StreamClientTransport(clientIn, clientOut), new McpClientOptions{ ClientInfo = new(){ Name="test", Version="0.0.0" } }, NullLoggerFactory.Instance) where clientIn/clientOut are the CROSSED ends of the same two pipes (server output -> client input).

title: Sim-mode tools never gate on IsRegistered — observational divergence from live
description: RequireContext() throws ContextNotSet (9006) when Context is null, but no chokepoint checks `IsRegistered`. In simulation mode you can call lacerte_field_write / lacerte_detail_write / lacerte_table_read without ever having called Register — all the gates pass, the sim store accepts the write, and the response says success. In live mode the bridge would reject with NotSignedIn (3) because the COM Register call is a hard prerequisite. The two-mode discipline rule in CLAUDE.md (`Simulation and live must be observationally identical for the happy path`) is violated for the most basic gate of all. CreateClient is the one path that *does* check IsRegistered (via SimulationStore.SimulateCreateClient since P14-030), but every other write/read path bypasses it.
recommendation: Add `if (!IsRegistered) throw new LacerteSDKError(StatusCodes.NotSignedIn, ...)` as the first synchronous gate after RequireContext() in WriteField, WriteDetail, and every Read* chokepoint. Sim mode honors this because Register() flips IsRegistered=true on the AccessGranted path. Add a regression test that confirms a fresh session manager rejects WriteField/ReadClient/etc with NotSignedIn before Register is called. The fix is one line per chokepoint plus a tiny test pass.
rationale: Round-1 P14-030 fixed CreateClient's sim-vs-live gate divergence but only for that one path. The same class of bug — sim skipping the IsRegistered latch — applies to every other chokepoint. This is exactly the kind of silent divergence the round-1 audit set out to eliminate, just missed across the rest of the surface.

verdict.reasoning: VERIFIED: The divergence is real and not addressed by Phase 14. Concrete read of LacerteSessionManager.cs confirms: (a) IsRegistered is a manager-side latch flipped true only on Register() AccessGranted (line 228, 244); (b) WriteField (line 645), WriteDetail (line 788), ListClients (459), ReadClient (488), ReadTableCore (519), ReadDetail (579), ReadEFStatus (600) all call only RequireContext() — none check IsRegistered. (c) The sim write helpers ApplySimFieldWrite / ApplySimDetailWrite go direct-to-ModuleStore, explicitly bypassing SimulationStore.SimulateFieldWrite per the comment at lines 1041-1047 — and SimulateFieldWrite is where the NotSignedIn-equivalent (`_sessionExpired`) gate lives (SimulationStore.cs:291). (d) Only CreateClient delegates to SimulationStore.SimulateCreateClient (post-P14-030), which performs the full IsRegistered gate at SimulationStore.cs:495-499. So the entire write+read surface except CreateClient skips the spec gate in sim. In live mode, the COM SDK itself will reject WriteField with NotSignedIn (203), so the divergence shows up as: sim returns Success, live returns NotSignedIn — exactly the kind of observational divergence CLAUDE.md "two-mode discipline" rule was written to prevent. Not a Phase-14 duplicate: P14-030 fixed only CreateClient; P14-003 covered live reads (which currently throw BridgeUnavailable, but that's a separate scaffolding issue); no Phase-14 task addresses a manager-side IsRegistered gate for WriteField/WriteDetail/Read*. Caveat on severity: read paths are currently unreachable in live mode anyway (P14-003 ThrowIfLiveUnwired), so the read divergence is latent until Phase 9 wires ODBC reads — but the write divergence (WriteField/WriteDetail) is reachable today because the live bridge IS wired for writes. The IsRegistered field also gates the AppId/Register lifecycle so adding a sim-side gate keeps the SessionStatus + idempotency cache semantics honest. Fix is one line per chokepoint plus tests — fully sim-only.
verdict.refinedRecommendation: Add a single private helper `RequireRegistered()` next to `RequireContext()` (around line 980) that throws `LacerteSDKError(StatusCodes.NotSignedIn, { ["reason"] = "Register() must succeed (AccessGranted) before this operation." })` when `!IsRegistered`. Call it as the first synchronous gate after `RequireContext()` in: WriteField (line 645), WriteDetail (788), ReadClient (488), ListClients (459), ReadTableCore (519), ReadDetail (579), ReadEFStatus (600). CreateClient already passes through SimulationStore.SimulateCreateClient which has its own gate, but adding the manager-side check there too is fine for uniformity. Do NOT switch the sim write helpers to delegate to SimulationStore.SimulateFieldWrite — the existing comment at LacerteSessionManager.cs:1041-1047 explains the gate-order intentionally lives at the manager (idempotency/access-map runs first), and the SimulationStore-side `_sessionExpired` latch handles the *expired* case separately from the *never-registered* case. The new manager-side IsRegistered check covers the "never registered" case which the sim store cannot see (its `_registered` field is set by SimulationStore.Register, which IS called from LacerteSessionManager.Register at line 241 — so flipping IsRegistered=true at the manager and `_registered=1` at the sim are coupled and the gate stays consistent). Tests: (1) `WriteField_BeforeRegister_ThrowsNotSignedIn` in LacerteSessionManagerTests.cs (sim); (2) `ReadClient_BeforeRegister_ThrowsNotSignedIn`; (3) `WriteDetail_BeforeRegister_ThrowsNotSignedIn`; (4) update FullFlowTests to confirm the happy path (Register → SetContext → Read/Write) still passes; (5) add one regression confirming SessionStatus snapshot still works pre-Register (it's an in-memory status read with no wire impact, so it must NOT gate on IsRegistered). Update DECISIONS.md with a brief entry "Sim-mode chokepoints gate on IsRegistered to match live SDK's NotSignedIn rejection" cross-referencing the CLAUDE.md two-mode rule. Tighten ARCHITECTURE.md Boundary Invariant #8 (or add #11) to read "Every wire chokepoint gates on IsRegistered before any access-map / idempotency / wire work — sim and live identical."

title: FieldWriteTools.value parameter accepts object? with no client-side type whitelist
description: Both write tools declare `object? value` with [Description] promising 'JSON-serializable scalar — string, number, or boolean.' Nothing enforces this. When the MCP host marshals a JSON array or object literal, the SDK deserializes to JsonElement (or a Dictionary/List) and rides into LacerteSessionManager.WriteField, then into the sim store as `row.Fields[field] = value` — which silently accepts any CLR value including a nested JsonElement Object. Round-1 P14-050's refined recommendation describes exactly this fix but the verdict was 'add a NormalizeFieldWriteValue in WriteField'; checking the source, no such normalizer was added. The whitelist gap remains. Also: there is no schema for `value` — the model has only the [Description] string to infer types, and the [McpServerTool] attribute does not emit a JSON Schema oneOf for the model.
recommendation: Implement the P14-050 refined recommendation: add a private `NormalizeFieldWriteValue(object? value, string field)` in LacerteSessionManager.WriteField that whitelists null/string/bool/sbyte..ulong/float/double/decimal/DateTime/JsonElement-of-primitive-kind and throws SyntheticStatusCodes.FieldWriteInvalid (or add a new 9009) on Array/Object JsonElement with {field, clrType} context. Run BEFORE BuildPayload so the rejection is logged in the same shape as other client-side rejects. Add tests covering: array value rejected, nested object rejected, JsonElement(string) accepted, JsonElement(number) accepted. The [Description] text already promises scalar-only — this just makes the promise enforceable.
rationale: Round-1 P14-050 was marked actionable in session but the actual code change (the NormalizeFieldWriteValue normalizer in LacerteSessionManager.WriteField) was not applied — only the DetailsTools text-validation half of the recommendation landed. This is a quality-of-fix concern on a round-1 finding: the refined recommendation explicitly called out the FieldWrite normalizer as half of the fix, and that half is still missing.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED: This is a half-fix on Phase-14 P14-050.

Evidence:
1. P14-050's refinedRecommendation in audit-findings.json explicitly had TWO numbered changes:
   (1) DetailsTools EnsureSafeText for detail-row strings — LANDED in src/LacertMCP.Server/Bridge/BridgeInputValidation.cs (EnsureSafeText helper called from ValidateWriteDetailArgs, plus ValidateValue for string-typed values).
   (2) NormalizeFieldWriteValue in LacerteSessionManager.WriteField to whitelist CLR types + reject JsonElement Array/Object — NOT LANDED.

2. Direct source evidence the second half is missing:

   - Grep for "JsonElement" in LacertMCP.Server source returns only DLL hits (no source references).
   - LacerteSessionManager.WriteField (lines 640-690) goes: RequireContext → RejectIfReadOnly → table 6/7 gate → ExecuteWithIdempotencyLock → BuildPayload/TryReplay → AssertWritable → WireLog.Record. No NormalizeFieldWriteValue anywhere.
   - ApplySimFieldWrite at line 1155 stores `row.Fields[field] = value` for any object.
   - The bridge layer is even self-aware about it: BridgeInputValidation.ValidateValue() (line 287-293) only checks string-typed values, with comment line 284-285: "Non-string values are accepted as-is at the bridge boundary — type whitelisting is the session-manager's job (see audit refinedRecommendation step 2)." 4. No test coverage: zero references to array-value rejection in FieldWriteToolsTests or any other test file.
